name: German
summary: German is a West Germanic, fusional language written in the Latin alphabet with ä, ö, ü and ß, in which every noun is capitalized. Its grammar lives in the noun phrase: three grammatical genders, four cases carried mostly by articles and adjectives, and adjective endings that change with the determiner (strong / weak / mixed). Its syntax is built around the verb's position – second in main clauses, first in yes/no questions, last in subordinate clauses – with the sentence bracket of modal + infinitive, auxiliary + participle and separable particles. Its lexicon splits meanings that Greek and English keep together (gehen / fahren, kennen / wissen, als / wenn / wann, zu / nach / in) and colours speech with modal particles and the du / Sie choice; three national standards (Germany, Austria, Switzerland) coexist.

Amtliches Regelwerk der deutschen Rechtschreibung (Rat für deutsche Rechtschreibung, 2006/2024)

phenomena.title: Latin alphabet with ä, ö, ü and ß
phenomena.what: German uses the 26 Latin letters plus the umlaut letters ä, ö, ü and the letter ß (Eszett). Umlauts are separate vowels, not accents: Mutter (mother) and Mütter (mothers) are different words. Without a German keyboard they are written ae, oe, ue and ss (Maedchen, Strasse) – acceptable in e-mails, wrong in careful writing. Turkish has the same ö and ü with the same sounds.

phenomena.title: ß or ss – and the spelling reform
phenomena.what: ß is written after a long vowel or a diphthong, ss after a short vowel (rule of the 1996 reform): heißen, Straße, aß – but dass, essen, isst. The same verb can switch: essen (short e) → er isst (short i) → er aß (long a). Switzerland and Liechtenstein never use ß (Strasse, heissen). Since 2017 a capital ẞ exists for all-caps text (STRASSE or STRAẞE). The reform of 1996 also replaced daß by dass and keeps three equal consonants in compounds (Brennnessel, Schifffahrt); older texts show the old spellings.

phenomena.title: Capital letters for every noun – and for polite Sie
phenomena.what: Every noun starts with a capital letter, also nouns made from other words (das Essen, das Gute, beim Kochen), while ich is small. The polite pronoun Sie and its forms Ihnen, Ihr are capitalized too; sie/ihr in small letters mean she, they, her, their, you (plural). So the capital decides the meaning of several homographs: morgen (tomorrow) – der Morgen (the morning), essen (to eat) – das Essen (the food, the meal), ihnen (to them) – Ihnen (to you, polite).

phenomena.title: Punctuation: commas by syntax, „…“, decimal comma, ordinal dot
phenomena.what: German commas follow the grammar, not the breath: every subordinate clause is separated by a comma (Ich weiß, dass er kommt), also relative clauses and most infinitive groups with um … zu. Quotation marks are „…“ (low–high) or »…«. Numbers use a decimal comma and a thousands point (1,5 · 1.000), and a dot after a number makes it an ordinal: am 3. Mai = am dritten Mai. Russian, Greek and Turkish share the decimal comma.

phenomena.title: Long and short vowels
phenomena.what: Vowel length distinguishes words: Staat (state) – Stadt (city), ihn (him) – in (in), Beet (flower bed) – Bett (bed). Spelling gives hints: a doubled vowel, h after the vowel and ie mark a long vowel; a doubled consonant marks a short one. Short vowels are also more open (in [ɪ] vs ihn [iː]).

phenomena.title: The vowels ö, ü (and ä)
phenomena.what: ö and ü are front rounded vowels: ü is i said with rounded lips, ö is e with rounded lips; each has a long and a short variant. ä is an open e. Greek, Russian and English lack ö and ü; Turkish has them with the same values.

phenomena.title: Two sounds of ch: ich and ach
phenomena.what: ch is [x] (a scrape at the back, as in Greek χα, Russian х) after a, o, u, au, and [ç] (a hiss at the front, as in Greek χέρι) after all other vowels and after consonants. The ending -ig is said [ɪç] in the standard of Germany (zwanzig), [ɪk] in the south and Austria. Greek χ alternates in exactly the same way.

phenomena.title: Final devoicing
phenomena.what: b, d, g (and s, v) at the end of a word or syllable are pronounced voiceless – p, t, k – but the spelling keeps b, d, g. Add an ending and the voiced sound comes back: Tag [taːk] – Tage [ˈtaːɡə]. Russian does the same (год [ɡot]); Turkish shows it even in spelling (kitap – kitabı).

phenomena.title: Letter–sound rules and the glottal stop
phenomena.what: German spelling is regular once a few rules are known: st and sp at the start of a word or stem are [ʃt], [ʃp]; z is [ts]; v is usually [f] and w is [v]; ei is [aɪ̯] but ie is [iː]; eu and äu are [ɔʏ̯]; s before a vowel is [z]; pf is one sound [p͡f]; r after a vowel and in -er becomes a vowel [ɐ]. A word or stem beginning with a vowel starts with an unwritten glottal stop [ʔ] (beobachten [bəˈʔoːbaxtn̩]), like Arabic hamza.

phenomena.title: Word stress: stem, prefixes, loanwords
phenomena.what: Native words stress the first syllable of the stem (ˈLehrer, ˈkaufen). Separable prefixes are stressed (ˈankommen), inseparable ones never (verˈlassen) – stress tells the two verb types apart. Compounds stress their first part (ˈKühlschrank). Many loanwords keep a final stress (Caˈfé, Büˈro, Universiˈtät); some words differ by country: Kaffee is ˈKaffee in Germany, Kaˈffee in Austria.

phenomena.title: Three grammatical genders
phenomena.what: Every noun is masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das), and the gender is grammatical: das Mädchen (girl) and das Kind are neuter, die Person is feminine for a man too. The gender chooses the article, dieser, the pronoun (der Tisch → er) and the adjective ending. Greek and Russian also have three genders, but a noun's gender often differs (ο τοίχος – die Wand, η καρέκλα – der Stuhl).

phenomena.title: Clues to the gender: suffixes, meaning classes, compounds
phenomena.what: Some endings decide the gender: -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -in are feminine; -chen, -lein neuter; -ling, -ismus masculine. Meaning classes help too: days, months and seasons are masculine (der Montag, der Mai, der Sommer). Most nouns in -e are feminine, with important exceptions (der Junge, der Name, der Käse, das Auge). A compound takes the gender of its last part.

phenomena.title: Same word, other gender, other meaning
phenomena.what: Some nouns exist with two genders, and each gender is a different word with its own meaning and often its own plural. The article is the only thing that tells them apart in writing.

phenomena.title: Plural classes – and the dative plural -n
phenomena.what: German has no single plural ending: -e (Tische), umlaut + -e (Stühle), -er with umlaut (Bücher), -(e)n (Frauen, Lampen), -nen after -in (Lehrerinnen), -s (Handys) and no ending, sometimes with umlaut only (Zimmer, Mütter). The plural is learned with the noun (der Stuhl, -¨e). The plural article is die for all genders, and ein has no plural. In the dative plural every noun ends in -n unless the plural already ends in -n or -s (mit den Kindern, but mit den Frauen, den Handys).

das Buch – die Bücher; die Lampe – die Lampen

phenomena.what: Umlaut (a → ä, o → ö, u → ü, au → äu) marks grammar in many places: noun plurals, comparison, the du/er present of some strong verbs, female nouns, diminutives and the Konjunktiv II. English keeps only relics (foot – feet, man – men).

phenomena.title: Four cases, shown mostly on the article
phenomena.what: German has four cases – nominative, accusative, dative, genitive. The noun itself changes little (dative plural -n, genitive -s, weak nouns -n); the case is carried by the article, the pronoun and the adjective ending. Only the masculine singular shows the accusative (der → den).

examples.text: der Tisch – den Tisch – dem Tisch – des Tisches
mit dem Bus, in der Küche

model.other: DET/PRON/NOUN/ADJ paradigms in language.json have all four cases; bank tokens are tagged with the case and checked against the forms.

phenomena.title: The genitive: -s/-es, Annas, von + dative
phenomena.what: Masculine and neuter nouns add -s or -es in the genitive singular (des Tisches, des Brots / des Brotes); feminine nouns add nothing (der Mutter). Names take -s without an apostrophe (Annas Buch). Spoken German often replaces the genitive with von + dative, and a few prepositions take the genitive (während, wegen, trotz).

phenomena.title: Female nouns in -in and gender-fair forms
phenomena.what: Most nouns for people have a female form in -in (plural -innen), often with umlaut: der Lehrer – die Lehrerin, der Arzt – die Ärztin, der Koch – die Köchin. phenomena.title: Compounds written as one word
phenomena.what: German joins words into one: the last part is the head and gives the gender and the plural; the first parts narrow it down. A linking element often stands between the parts (-s-, -n-, -en-, -er-). Compounds are written as one word and stressed on the first part.

phenomena.title: Any word can become a noun
phenomena.what: An infinitive becomes a neuter noun (das Essen, das Kochen), an adjective a noun with adjective endings (das Gute, etwas Neues); both are capitalized. beim + infinitive means ‘while doing’.

phenomena.title: Possessives: the owner picks the word, the noun picks the ending
phenomena.what: mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr replace the article and take the endings of ein (with a plural: meine). Two separate choices: the owner chooses sein (his, its) or ihr (her, their), the owned noun the ending: seine Frau (his wife), ihr Mann (her husband). Greek puts μου after the noun with the article (η μητέρα μου); German never adds an article.

examples.text: Anna und ihr Bruder – Max und seine Schwester

examples.note: euer drops its e before an ending

model.other: DET.poss (16 cells), 7 lexemes incl. de:Ihr.poss; inflect class poss; transform Number and Formality.

phenomena.title: Personal pronouns in three cases
phenomena.what: Personal pronouns have their own accusative and dative forms: ich – mich – mir, du – dich – dir, er – ihn – ihm, sie – sie – ihr, wir – uns – uns, ihr – euch – euch, sie – sie – ihnen, Sie – Sie – Ihnen. The genitive forms (meiner, deiner) survive only in fixed phrases.

examples.text: Ich mag dich. – Ich helfe dir.

model.other: PRON paradigm with NOM/ACC/DAT; inflect PRON;ACC (fn.object), PRON;DAT (fn.case); wer has NOM/ACC/DAT/GEN (class intp).

phenomena.title: er, sie, es follow the noun's gender, not the sex
phenomena.what: A pronoun copies the grammatical gender of its noun: der Tisch → er, die Lampe → sie, das Buch → es, every plural → sie. With das Mädchen the grammar asks for es, though people often switch to sie once they know her name.

examples.text: Wo ist der Schlüssel? – Er ist auf dem Tisch.

model.other: Taught in fn.pronoun.subject (callout “Things are er, sie or es”); profile senses of de:er, de:sie, de:es say ‘it’ for nouns of that gender.

phenomena.title: man – the impersonal ‘one, you, people’
phenomena.what: man is the everyday impersonal subject: ‘one, you, people, they’. It takes the er-form of the verb and has the object forms einen, einem; it is never replaced by er. Greek and Russian use a plural verb without a subject instead (λένε, говорят).

examples.text: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
examples.note: How do you say that in German?

phenomena.gap: A lexeme de:man (PRON, forms man/einen/einem) and a function (impersonal statements) with bank sentences.

phenomena.title: es as an empty subject; es gibt
phenomena.what: German needs a subject even when nobody acts: es is an empty subject with weather verbs (es regnet), in fixed phrases (Wie geht es dir?) and in es gibt (there is). Greek and Russian simply have no subject here (βρέχει, идёт дождь). ‘There is / are’ is es gibt + accusative (Es gibt hier einen Park) – not haben or sein.

examples.note: how are you? (literally: how goes it to you)

phenomena.record: A fixed construction (lexeme es_gibt or a frame), not a word property.

model.other: Profile sense s2 of de:es (“an empty subject or placeholder”); the greeting lexemes de:wie_geht_es_dir / de:wie_geht_es_Ihnen; fn.have callout “There is is es gibt”. fn.have callout and trap; geben is not a course lexeme.

phenomena.gap: es gibt + accusative as a construction with bank sentences (fd.06); weather verbs come with a weather field. A lexeme for geben (or a construction lexeme es gibt) with bank sentences in fd.06 / fd.11.

phenomena.title: Reflexive verbs and pronouns: sich
phenomena.what: Many verbs need a reflexive pronoun: mich, dich, sich, uns, euch, sich (accusative) or mir, dir, sich (dative when there is another object). Some verbs are only reflexive (sich freuen), others change meaning (verlassen → sich verlassen auf, to rely on).

examples.note: sich verlassen auf = to rely on (de:verlassen sense)

phenomena.record: features.reflexive: [{case: ACC | DAT, senses}] – the meanings that need the reflexive pronoun, or none.

model.other: Every verb states it; one reflexive meaning in the course: de:verlassen s3 (sich verlassen auf).

phenomena.gap: Reflexive pronoun forms (PRON cells with REFL) and the cr.07 lesson.

phenomena.title: Relative pronouns der, die, das (dessen, denen)
phenomena.what: Relative clauses start with der, die, das in the gender and number of the noun and the case of their role in the clause; the verb goes to the end. The forms are the article's, except dessen, deren (genitive) and denen (dative plural).

examples.text: die Frau, deren Sohn Arzt ist

model.other: Profile senses only (de:was ‘alles, was …’, de:wo ‘die Stadt, wo ich wohne’, de:welcher relative).

phenomena.gap: A relative-pronoun lexeme (PRON.rel paradigm) and the cr.06 lesson with `combine`.

phenomena.title: da- and wo- compounds: darauf, worauf
phenomena.what: A preposition with a pronoun for a thing becomes da(r)- + preposition (darauf, damit, dafür), in questions wo(r)- (worauf, womit). For persons the preposition + pronoun stays: auf ihn, auf wen.

examples.text: Ich warte auf den Bus. → Ich warte darauf.
Worauf wartest du? – Auf wen wartest du?

phenomena.record: Each da-/wo- form as a lexeme linked to its preposition.
phenomena.gap: Lexemes (or a derived table per preposition) and a lesson after the verbs with prepositional objects.

phenomena.title: Strong, weak and mixed adjective endings
phenomena.what: Before a noun an adjective always has an ending, chosen by the word in front of it: after der/dieser (weak) only -e or -en; after ein/kein/mein without an ending (mixed) the adjective shows the gender itself (-er, -es); with no article (strong) it takes the article's ending. In the dative the ending after any article is -en. A few adjectives change their stem when they take an ending: ein hohes Haus, ein dunkles Bier, ein teures Auto.

examples.text: der große Tisch – ein großer Tisch – großer Hunger
mit dem neuen Auto, in einer kleinen Wohnung
zwei kleine Kinder – die kleinen Kinder

phenomena.record: features.adjAfter on determiners (weak | mixed | strong) and features.stem on adjectives (hoh-, dunkl-, teur-, or none).

model.other: Every determiner states the adjective declension it triggers (der, dieser, jener, alle, manche, welcher → weak; ein, kein, the possessives → mixed; viel, wenig, einige, ein bisschen, wie viel(e) → strong); every adjective its stem before an ending. language.json ADJ paradigm: 12 cells × STRG/WEAK/MIX; fn.adjective inflect generators.

phenomena.gap: No genitive adjective cells; the app does not yet generate or check article + adjective + noun phrases from adjAfter.

phenomena.title: Predicative and adverbial adjectives do not change
phenomena.what: After sein, werden, bleiben the adjective has no ending (Das Haus ist groß), and the same bare form is the adverb – German has no -ly: Er fährt schnell. Greek and Russian make the predicate agree (το σπίτι είναι μεγάλο) and have separate adverbs.

model.other: ADJ citation cell ‘ADJ’; fn.agreement callout “After sein: no ending”.

phenomena.title: Comparison: -er, am -sten, umlaut, irregulars
phenomena.what: The comparative adds -er (+ als), the superlative is am …-sten (predicate, adverb) or der …-ste (before a noun). Short adjectives often add umlaut; a few are irregular. Equality is so … wie.

examples.text: gut – besser – am besten; viel – mehr – am meisten; hoch – höher – am höchsten
Der Zug ist schneller als der Bus.

phenomena.record: features.comparison (ADJ: regular | umlaut | irregular | not compared; ADV: [comparative, superlative] or none); the ADJ forms in ADJ;CMPR, ADJ;SPRL.

model.other: ADJ;CMPR, ADJ;SPRL and four weak superlative cells; fn.comparison generators (inflect, bank).

phenomena.title: Adjectives without endings: rosa, lila, orange, Berliner
phenomena.what: A few colour words borrowed from other languages (rosa, lila, orange, beige) take no endings in careful German (ein rosa Kleid); speech often adds them. Adjectives from place names in -er never change (der Berliner Bahnhof, Neuseeländer Spinat).

model.other: class inv on de:rosa, de:lila, de:orange (paradigm ADJ.inv = one cell); fn.comparison trap.

phenomena.title: Present tense: endings, stem-vowel change, no progressive
phenomena.what: The present adds -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en to the stem; polite Sie takes the plural form. There is one present for ‘I eat’, ‘I am eating’ and often ‘I will eat’. There is no progressive; speech adds gerade or, colloquially, am + infinitive (Ich bin am Kochen). Many strong verbs change the stem vowel in the du and er forms only: essen → isst, fahren → fährt, laufen → läuft (the imperative keeps i but drops the umlaut: Iss! Fahr!).

examples.text: ich kaufe, du kaufst, er kauft, wir kaufen, ihr kauft, sie kaufen

phenomena.record: features.presentChange: no change | e>i | e>ie | a>ä | au>äu | irregular.

model.other: VERB paradigm cells (all required); inflect over all known verbs (separable ones excluded). fn.present callout “No -ing form”. Forms stored; inflect generators for essen/mögen/wollen (fn.present) and fahren/laufen/verlassen (fn.direction); imperative traps.

phenomena.title: Weak, strong and mixed verbs; principal parts
phenomena.what: Weak verbs form the past with -te and the participle ge-…-t (kaufen – kaufte – gekauft). Strong verbs change the stem vowel (ablaut) and form the participle in -en (trinken – trank – getrunken). Mixed verbs change the vowel and take weak endings (rennen – rannte – gerannt). Inseparable prefixes and -ieren verbs have no ge- (verlassen, studiert). The principal parts are learned with each strong verb, as in English sing – sang – sung.

examples.text: trinken – trank – getrunken; gehen – ging – gegangen

examples.note: no ge- after an inseparable prefix

phenomena.record: features.principalParts (infinitive, 3 SG present, 3 SG Präteritum, Partizip II) and features.conjugation: weak | strong | mixed | modal | irregular.

model.other: All 23 verbs state their four principal parts (separable ones with the particle: kommt an, kam an, angekommen) and their class; every verb now stores V;PST;3;SG (the 5 separable verbs had none). langcore principalParts still shows only the du/er forms and the auxiliary.

phenomena.gap: The word card does not show the Präteritum and the Partizip II from principalParts yet; no ablaut series; V;PST;3;SG and V;PTCP;PST are not required cells in language.json.

phenomena.title: Modal verbs
phenomena.what: können, müssen, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen (and möchte) have no ending in ich and er and a different vowel in the singular; the second verb goes to the end in the infinitive without zu. English modals behave alike (he can, no -s).

examples.text: ich will – er will; ich mag – er mag
ich kann, er muss, du darfst

model.other: conjugation “modal” on de:wollen and de:mögen (with möchte cells V;SBJV;PST and senseForms); fn.present table and flow block.

phenomena.gap: können, müssen, dürfen, sollen (cr.04); lassen and the bare infinitive after gehen / bleiben are not marked.

phenomena.title: Separable verbs
phenomena.what: A stressed particle (an, ab, auf, aus, ein, mit, weg, zurück, her-, hin- …) belongs to the verb but goes to the end of a main clause; in a subordinate clause and in the infinitive it is joined again; ge- and zu go between particle and stem (angekommen, anzukommen). Hungarian and Dutch have this; none of the course or known languages do. The particle often changes the meaning unpredictably: ankommen (arrive) – es kommt darauf an (it depends).

examples.text: ankommen: Der Zug kommt um acht an.
…, weil der Zug um acht ankommt.
Der Zug kommt an. – Es kommt darauf an.

phenomena.record: features.separable: the particle, or none.

model.other: 5 verbs with `separable` and a V;SEP cell (extraTags SEP); the tokenizer reads the particle as a V;SEP token (21 in the bank); inflect skips separable verbs unless listed, because one cell holds only the stem form. particleVerbs lists on 14 lexemes; 5 separable verb lexemes.

phenomena.gap: No zu-infinitive cell; no drill of the whole form (kommt … an) and of the particle position; particle verbs listed in profiles are not lexemes.

phenomena.title: Inseparable prefixes – and prefixes that can be both
phenomena.what: These prefixes never separate, are never stressed and block ge- in the participle. They often change the meaning or make a verb transitive: verlassen (leave a place, + accusative) vs weggehen. durch-, über-, um-, unter- can be either: übersetzen (translate, inseparable) – übersetzen (ferry across, separable).

examples.text: verlassen – Ich verlasse das Haus. – Ich habe das Haus verlassen.
Er fährt den Baum um. – Er umfährt den Stau.

phenomena.record: features.inseparable: be | emp | ent | er | ge | miss | ver | zer, or none.

model.other: de:verlassen states ver- (participle verlassen, no ge-); every other verb says none.

phenomena.gap: Only one verb with an inseparable prefix in the course; no drill that contrasts separable and inseparable verbs, and no stress information (no ipa).

phenomena.title: Perfect with haben or sein
phenomena.what: The perfect uses haben for most verbs and sein for verbs of motion or change of state without an object (gehen, fahren, kommen, bleiben, sein). A verb can take both: Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren / Ich habe das Auto gefahren. South German and Austrian use sein also with stehen, sitzen, liegen.

examples.text: Ich bin nach Hause gegangen. Ich bin hier geblieben.
Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren. – Ich habe das Auto gefahren.
examples.note: fahren: sein without object, haben with one

phenomena.record: features.aux: haben | sein | both, and features.auxBySense: [{aux, senses, when?}] for the verbs whose auxiliary depends on the meaning or on a direct object.

model.other: All 23 verbs: 12 sein, 10 haben, 1 both (de:fahren: haben with a direct object, s1; sein without one, s1–s3); principalParts shows ‘perfect with …’.

phenomena.gap: The perfect itself is taught in cr.01; south German / Austrian sein with stehen, sitzen, liegen is not recorded (those verbs are not course words).

phenomena.title: Perfekt in speech, Präteritum in writing
phenomena.what: Spoken German tells the past mostly with the perfect (Ich habe gegessen), written narrative with the Präteritum (Er aß). sein, haben and the modals use the Präteritum in speech too (war, hatte, wollte). The south uses the perfect almost only; the north uses more Präteritum.

model.other: war is used in fn.time.day (5 V;PST tokens in the bank); otherwise cr.01.

phenomena.gap: Full Präteritum paradigms (at least sein, haben, modals) and the Perfekt lesson cr.01 with the register note.

phenomena.title: The future: present + time word, or werden
phenomena.what: With a time word the present already means the future (Morgen komme ich zurück). werden + infinitive marks the future or a guess (Er wird schon zu Hause sein). werden alone means ‘to become’ (Ich werde Lehrerin).

model.other: fn.time.day and fn.present say that the present covers the future.

phenomena.gap: werden as a lexeme (auxiliary and full verb) and cr.02.

phenomena.title: Konjunktiv II: politeness and unreal conditions
phenomena.what: Konjunktiv II makes polite requests (möchte, hätte gern, könnten Sie) and unreal conditions (Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich kommen). Most verbs use würde + infinitive; sein, haben, modals and a few strong verbs use their own forms (wäre, hätte, könnte).

examples.text: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich kommen.

model.other: V;SBJV;PST cells only for de:mögen (möchte); 8 bank tokens.

phenomena.gap: Konjunktiv II of sein, haben, modals and würde; cr.05.

phenomena.title: Konjunktiv I: reported speech
phenomena.what: Newspapers and formal reports mark what someone else said with Konjunktiv I: er sei, er habe, er komme. In speech the indicative or Konjunktiv II is used instead.

examples.text: Sie sagte, sie habe keine Zeit.
examples.note: she said she had no time

phenomena.gap: Konjunktiv I cells (at least 3 SG) and a reading-level lesson.

phenomena.title: Two passives: werden and sein
phenomena.what: werden + participle describes an action being done (Vorgangspassiv), sein + participle the resulting state (Zustandspassiv). The doer is von + dative.

examples.text: Das Buch wurde von Goethe geschrieben.

phenomena.gap: werden lexeme and a passive lesson with `transform` (active ↔ passive).

phenomena.title: Three imperatives: du, ihr, Sie
phenomena.what: One person you say du to: the stem (Komm! Geh! Warte!); several: the ihr form (Kommt!); anyone you say Sie to: infinitive + Sie (Kommen Sie!). Let's = wir form with the verb first (Gehen wir!).

model.other: IMP cells for 18 verbs (not heißen, haben, mögen, wollen, kochen); formsAlt holds Gehe!/Komme!; transform Mood and Formality (8 + bank).

phenomena.title: Infinitive with and without zu
phenomena.what: Most verbs, nouns and adjectives take zu + infinitive at the end of the clause (Ich habe keine Zeit zu kochen); um … zu means ‘in order to’. Modals (and lassen, gehen, sehen, hören) take the bare infinitive. With a separable verb zu goes inside: anzukommen.

examples.text: Ich habe keine Zeit zu kochen.
Ich gehe in die Stadt, um Brot zu kaufen.

model.other: Profile sense of de:zu; modal + bare infinitive in fn.present.

phenomena.gap: A zu-infinitive cell for separable verbs and a lesson (cr.04 / later).

phenomena.title: Verb second in statements, verb first in yes/no questions and commands
phenomena.what: In a statement the conjugated verb is always the second element. Anything can come first – the subject, a time word, an object, a whole subordinate clause – and then the subject moves behind the verb. English keeps only relics (Never have I …); Greek, Russian and Turkish order words freely. A yes/no question and a command put the verb first, with no helper like English ‘do’ (Trinkst du Tee? Kommen Sie herein!).

examples.text: Ich trinke heute Tee. – Heute trinke ich Tee. – Tee trinke ich heute.
examples.note: the verb stays in place two

examples.text: Am Montag gehe ich zur Arbeit.
Weil es kalt ist, trinken wir Tee.
examples.note: a clause in first place, then the verb
the second verb stays at the end

model.other: Bank sentences carry `alts` for other correct orders; build_sentence checks the order against text + alts; fn.present callout “Verb second”. transform Mood INT (42 bank variants) and IMP (8); word_order on yes/no questions.

phenomena.title: Verb at the end of subordinate clauses
phenomena.what: After weil, dass, wenn, als, ob, obwohl, after question words in indirect questions and in relative clauses, the conjugated verb goes to the end; a separable verb joins its particle there, a modal comes last. Spoken German often keeps main-clause order after weil (weil ich habe Durst) – common, but wrong in writing. Turkish puts the verb at the end of every clause.

examples.text: …, weil der Zug um acht ankommt.
Ich weiß nicht, wann er kommt.

model.other: fn.connectors (40 bank sentences) with the three connector groups and the spoken-weil callout.

phenomena.title: The sentence bracket (Satzklammer)
phenomena.what: The finite verb in second place and the rest of the verb at the end frame the sentence: a modal + infinitive, a separable verb + particle, the perfect auxiliary + participle, werden + infinitive. Everything else stands inside the bracket, however long.

examples.text: Ich will heute Abend Tee trinken.
Der Zug kommt um acht Uhr an.

model.other: Modal brackets (fd.07) and separable brackets (fd.13) appear in the bank; no exercise asks for the slot of the second verb part.

phenomena.gap: A `word_order` generator that removes the bracket's second part and asks where it goes; perfect and passive brackets after cr.01.

phenomena.title: Order inside the sentence: time – manner – place; pronouns first
phenomena.what: Between the verb and the end, time usually comes before manner and place (‘te-ka-mo-lo’), pronouns come before nouns, a dative noun before an accusative noun but an accusative pronoun before a dative pronoun, and nicht stands before what it negates or at the end.

examples.text: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Bus nach Berlin.
Ich gebe dem Kind das Buch. – Ich gebe es ihm.
examples.note: nouns: dative first; pronouns: accusative first

examples.text: Ich esse den Fisch nicht. – Das ist nicht gut.
examples.note: nicht at the end / before the adjective

model.other: fn.time.day (“time comes before manner and place”); fn.negation (position of nicht).

phenomena.gap: Object order (dative/accusative, pronouns) comes only with cr.03; no exercise targets the order of the middle field.

phenomena.title: nicht or kein – and only one negation
phenomena.what: kein (a negative article, declined like ein, with a plural) negates a noun that would have ein or no article; nicht negates everything else – verbs, adjectives, places, and nouns with der, dieser or a possessive. Only one negative word per clause: Ich esse nichts (Greek δεν … τίποτα and Russian ничего не … double it).

examples.text: Ich habe kein Brot. – Ich trinke keinen Kaffee.

model.other: de:kein (class neg, 16 cells), de:nicht; transform Polarity (49 bank variants). fn.negation callout “Only one negation”; lexemes de:nichts, de:niemand, de:nie, de:niemals, de:weder, de:noch.

phenomena.title: doch – ‘yes’ against a negative
phenomena.what: To contradict a negative question or statement, German answers doch, not ja. Arabic بَلَى (balā) and French si work the same; Greek, Russian, Turkish and English have no special word.

examples.text: Du kommst nicht mit? – Doch, ich komme mit.

model.other: de:doch (PART, role); fn.question.yesno callout.

phenomena.title: Prepositions fix the case
phenomena.what: Each preposition takes a fixed case: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu + dative; bis, durch, für, gegen, ohne, um + accusative; während, wegen, trotz + genitive (spoken often dative). Greek prepositions take the accusative (με τον αδερφό μου) – German mit takes the dative (mit meinem Bruder).

examples.text: für meinen Vater, ohne meinen Bruder

phenomena.record: features.governs: [{case, senses?, when?}] – the case of each meaning of the preposition (two-way: DAT for where?, ACC for where to?); a contraction states the case of its article.

model.other: Every ADP states the case per meaning: über ACC for “about” (s1), DAT for “above” (s2), ACC for “across / via”; in and an DAT for the time senses (im Mai, am Montag); während GEN (everyday DAT noted); meanings that are not prepositional (zu “too”, auf “open”) are in no item.

phenomena.title: Two-way prepositions: Wo? dative, Wohin? accusative
phenomena.what: in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen take the dative for a place (Wo?) and the accusative for a goal (Wohin?). Russian в / на work the same way (в парке / в парк).

examples.text: Ich bin im Park. – Ich gehe in den Park.
Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch. – Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.

model.other: governs per meaning on 9 two-way prepositions (DAT for where?, ACC for where to?, and the one-case meanings: über “about” + ACC, an / in for time + DAT); fn.prep.place and fn.direction with bank sentences.

phenomena.gap: The `contrast` exercise (Akk vs Dat with the reason) is not implemented.

phenomena.title: Verbs that govern a case or a preposition
phenomena.what: Most verbs take an accusative object, but some take the dative (helfen, danken, gehören, gefallen, antworten) or a fixed preposition with a fixed case (warten auf + accusative, denken an + accusative, sich freuen über / auf). These have to be learned with the verb.
phenomena.record: features.governs: [{case, prep?, senses, note?}] – the object cases, prepositional objects and predicative nominatives of each meaning, or none.

model.other: Every verb states its frame per meaning: kaufen ACC (+ DAT), warten auf + ACC (s1) / ACC (s2 maintain), ankommen auf + ACC (s2) / bei + DAT (s3), gehen DAT (s4 es geht mir gut), heißen NOM (predicative).

phenomena.gap: Dative verbs (helfen, gefallen) come in cr.03; no drill ‘which case after this verb’.

phenomena.title: Body states: Mir ist kalt, Ich habe Hunger
phenomena.what: Feelings of the body and impersonal states take the person in the dative: Mir ist kalt (I'm cold – Ich bin kalt means ‘I am a cold person’), Mir ist schlecht (I feel sick), Wie geht es dir?, Das gefällt mir. Russian мне холодно and Hebrew קַר לִי are built the same way. Hunger and thirst use haben + a bare noun: Ich habe Hunger, Ich habe Durst (also Angst, Zeit, Recht haben).

examples.note: I'm hungry (hungrig sein is more formal)

model.other: fn.adjective and fn.copula traps; the greeting lexemes with dir / Ihnen. de:Hunger, de:Durst (NOUN, senses [], role) beside de:hungrig, de:durstig; fn.have callout.

phenomena.gap: Bank sentences with Mir ist kalt/warm/schlecht and a transform (person change); gefallen in cr.03. Angst, Recht, Glück, Zeit are not lexemes; the collocation is not a stored unit.

phenomena.title: Preposition + article in one word: im, zum, zur …
phenomena.what: Some prepositions merge with dem, der or das: im, am, beim, vom, zum (dem), zur (der), ins, ans (das). The merged form is the normal one; in dem Park sounds like ‘in that park’. Speech also says aufm, unterm, hinterm. Greek merges σε + τον → στον the same way.

examples.text: in dem → im Park; zu der → zur Schule

phenomena.record: features.contractions: [{form, article, lexeme?, register?}] on the preposition, or none; the contractions themselves are lexemes with role.

model.other: Every preposition lists its merged forms (in → im, ins; zu → zum, zur; auf → aufs; für → fürs; um → ums; colloquial: übers, überm, unterm, unters, vorm, vors, hinterm, hinters); the 8 merged forms of the course (de:im … de:vom) are lexemes with role and are linked from their preposition.

phenomena.title: Where German uses an article and where not
phenomena.what: No article with a job, role or nationality after sein (Ich bin Lehrerin), with mass nouns in general (Ich trinke Wasser) and with most country names (nach Griechenland). An article with feminine and plural country names (in die Türkei, in der Schweiz, in den USA), with months and seasons (im Mai) and, in colloquial southern German, with first names (der Peter) – Greek uses the article with every name (ο Πέτρος).

model.other: Callouts in fn.copula (no article with jobs), fn.object (food and drink), fn.direction (in die Türkei); profile sense of de:der (der Peter).

phenomena.gap: Country names are not course words; no exercise contrasts ‘article / no article’.

phenomena.title: Das ist / Das sind / Das bin ich
phenomena.what: In pointing sentences with das, the verb agrees with the noun or pronoun that follows, not with das: Das sind meine Eltern. Das bin ich.

examples.text: Das ist ein Kind. – Das sind Kinder.
Das bin ich. – Das sind wir.

phenomena.title: Long attributes before the noun
phenomena.what: A participle with its own objects and adverbs can stand between the article and the noun: der um acht Uhr ankommende Zug (the train arriving at eight). It is frequent in written German; Russian and Turkish use the same prenominal type.

phenomena.title: seit + present for something still going on
phenomena.what: Something that started in the past and still goes on is said in the present with seit: Ich wohne seit drei Jahren hier. English uses the present perfect (I have lived).

phenomena.title: Habit adverbs in -s: montags, morgens, abends
phenomena.what: A day or part of the day + -s, written small, means ‘every …, on …s’: montags (on Mondays), morgens, abends, nachts. With a clock time morgens/abends act as a.m./p.m.

phenomena.title: gehen, fahren, fliegen: the verb shows how you move
phenomena.what: German chooses the verb of movement by the means: gehen on foot, fahren by any vehicle (also as a passenger), fliegen by plane. Ich gehe nach Berlin sounds like walking there. Russian splits идти / ехать the same way; Greek πάω, Turkish gitmek and English go cover all.

phenomena.title: stellen / legen / setzen / hängen – stehen / liegen / sitzen / hängen
phenomena.what: Putting something somewhere and its being there are said with pairs that encode the position: upright (stellen → stehen), lying (legen → liegen), sitting (setzen → sitzen), hanging (hängen → hängen). The causing verb is weak and takes the accusative with two-way prepositions; the state verb is strong and takes the dative. Russian has the same system (ставить/стоять, класть/лежать, сажать/сидеть, вешать/висеть); Greek uses βάζω and είναι.

examples.text: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch. – Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
Ich stelle die Flasche in den Kühlschrank. – Die Flasche steht im Kühlschrank.
Ich setze das Kind auf den Stuhl. – Das Kind sitzt auf dem Stuhl.
Das Bild hängt an der Wand.

phenomena.title: kennen, wissen, können – three ‘know’
phenomena.what: kennen is to be acquainted with a person, place or thing (Ich kenne Anna); wissen is to know a fact (Ich weiß, wo sie wohnt), with a clause or das/es/alles; können is to know how to do something or a language (Ich kann Deutsch). Hebrew לְהַכִּיר / לָדַעַת and Turkish tanımak / bilmek split the same way.

phenomena.title: hin and her: away from me, towards me
phenomena.what: Directional words mark the speaker's point of view: her- means towards the speaker, hin- away from the speaker (herein / hinein, herauf / hinauf). Spoken German shortens both to r- (rein, rauf). The question words split the same way: Wo gehst du hin? = Wohin gehst du?

phenomena.title: One English or Greek word, several German ones
phenomena.what: German divides several common meanings that English and Greek keep together: when (wenn / als / wann), if (wenn / ob), because (weil / denn), to (zu / nach / in), at (an / bei / in / auf), from (aus / von), holiday (Urlaub / Ferien), hour (Stunde / Uhr). Each choice follows one question (past or not? whether or condition? kind of place?). The full list is in `distinctions`.

phenomena.title: Homonyms and polysemy
phenomena.what: Many common words have meanings that are separate concepts: Bank (bank / bench), Schloss (castle / lock), Zug (train / move / draught), leicht (easy / light). Some differ in plural or gender (see the polysemy list).

examples.text: Ich gehe zur Bank. – Ich sitze auf der Bank.

phenomena.title: Cognates, loans and false friends
phenomena.what: Some German words look like English or Greek words but mean something else: Handy (mobile phone), also (so, therefore), Gift (poison), bekommen (to get), will (want), Chef (boss), eventuell (possibly); for a Greek speaker Apotheke is a pharmacy, not a storeroom (αποθήκη). Most look-alikes are true cognates or loans (Haus – house, Schule ← σχολή, Rucksack → рюкзак) – the bridges to the learner's languages.

phenomena.title: Register: du-words and Sie-words, Oma and Großmutter
phenomena.what: Many meanings have a neutral or formal word and a colloquial one: Großmutter – Oma, Universität – Uni, auf Wiedersehen – tschüss, Guten Tag – hallo, Mobiltelefon – Handy. Choosing wrongly is a social mistake, not a grammar one.

phenomena.title: Collocations and noun–verb phrases (Funktionsverbgefüge)
phenomena.what: Many nouns go with one fixed verb that has little meaning of its own: eine Frage stellen, eine Entscheidung treffen, Platz nehmen. Formal German likes these phrases.

phenomena.title: Kinship terms
phenomena.what: German kinship words do not say which side of the family (Onkel, Tante, Großvater for both sides – Arabic splits them) but do mark the sex of cousins (Cousin / Cousine). Oma / Opa are the everyday words, Großmutter / Großvater the neutral ones; Eltern and Großeltern are plural only.

phenomena.title: du, ihr and Sie
phenomena.what: du (one person) and ihr (several) for family, friends, children and, increasingly, colleagues; Sie – capitalized, with the verb of ‘they’, for one or many – for adults you do not know well. Switching to du is offered by the older or higher-ranking person (das Du anbieten). The choice changes the pronoun, the possessive, the verb, the imperative and the greeting.

phenomena.title: Greetings by time of day and region
phenomena.what: Guten Morgen / Tag / Abend by the time of day, Gute Nacht only when parting late. Regions have their own: Grüß Gott and Servus in Bavaria and Austria, Moin in the north, Grüezi in Switzerland. At noon colleagues greet each other with Mahlzeit!, at table Guten Appetit!

phenomena.title: Modal particles: ja, doch, mal, denn, halt …
phenomena.what: Small unstressed words in the middle of the sentence add the speaker's attitude: ja (as we know), doch (come on / after all), mal (just, softens a request), denn (in questions: interest, impatience), halt / eben (that's how it is), schon, wohl, vielleicht (amazement). They are hard to translate but make German sound natural. Russian же, ведь, -то are similar.

phenomena.title: Polite requests
phenomena.what: A bare imperative can sound sharp; polite German uses bitte, Konjunktiv II (möchte, hätte gern, könnten Sie) and softeners (mal, vielleicht). Danke alone after an offer often means ‘no, thank you’.

phenomena.title: Herr, Frau and titles
phenomena.what: Adults are addressed as Herr / Frau + surname with Sie; Frau is used for every woman whatever her marital status (Fräulein is obsolete). Academic titles are part of the address: Frau Dr. Weber.

examples.text: Herr Müller, kommen Sie bitte herein!

phenomena.title: Germany, Austria, Switzerland: one language, three standards
phenomena.what: German has three national standards with their own words and spellings (Austrian Jänner, Paradeiser, Erdapfel; Swiss ss for ß, Rüebli), and strong dialects; in German-speaking Switzerland people speak Swiss German dialects and write Standard German – a diglossia comparable, on a smaller scale, to Arabic.

phenomena.title: Meals and food culture
phenomena.what: Frühstück, Mittagessen, Abendessen – in many families the evening meal is a cold one (Abendbrot); Kaffee und Kuchen is an afternoon meal of its own, especially on Sundays. Mahlzeit! greets colleagues at noon, Guten Appetit! starts a meal.

phenomena.title: Week, date and clock conventions
phenomena.what: The week starts on Monday and weeks are numbered (KW 41 = Kalenderwoche 41); dates are day.month.year (08.10.2026); written and official times use the 24-hour clock (um 20 Uhr), while speech often uses 12 hours (um acht Uhr abends).

examples.text: um 20 Uhr – um acht Uhr abends

phenomena.gap: The date (ordinal numbers) and the 24-hour clock are not taught; no `date` / `clock` exercise.

phenomena.title: Number words: einundzwanzig, eins / ein, Milliarde
phenomena.what: Between the tens German says the unit first, joined with und, in one word: 21 = einundzwanzig (‘one-and-twenty’). Long numbers are written as one word too. Arabic also puts the unit first (wāḥid wa-ʿišrūn); Greek, Russian, Turkish, Hebrew and English put the tens first. sechs and sieben lose letters in sechzehn, sechzig, siebzehn, siebzig. ‘One’ is eins when counting but the declined article ein before a noun; on the phone zwei becomes zwo. Large numbers follow the long scale: Milliarde = 10⁹ (English billion), Billion = 10¹².

examples.text: ein Stuhl, eine Tasse, einen Stuhl

phenomena.title: Telling the time: halb neun = 8:30
phenomena.what: halb counts towards the next hour: halb neun is 8:30. Viertel nach / Viertel vor are quarter past / to; in the east and south viertel neun is 8:15 and dreiviertel neun 8:45. Uhr is the clock time, Stunde a duration. Russian половина девятого counts the same way.

phenomena.title: Ordinal numbers and dates
phenomena.what: Ordinals add -te up to 19 and -ste from 20 and decline like adjectives; erste, dritte, siebte (and achte) are irregular. Written as a number with a dot: der 3. Mai = der dritte Mai, am 3. Mai = am dritten Mai.

NOUN.title: gender
NOUN.why: Chooses the article (der / die / das), the pronoun and the adjective endings; learned with every noun. Plural-only nouns (class plt) have none.

NOUN.title: plural, per meaning
NOUN.why: The plural is not predictable and is learned with the noun; a meaning may have its own plural (Banken / Bänke) or none (das Land = the countryside). A meaning left out of every item has no plural. none: mass nouns (class sgt) and plural-only nouns (class plt).

NOUN.title: singular declension
NOUN.why: strong: des Tisches, dem Tisch (-(e)s in the genitive); weak (n-declension): den / dem / des Jungen; mixed: des Namens, den Namen; feminine: no ending in the singular; adjectival: declined like an adjective (der Verwandte, ein Verwandter).

NOUN.title: compound parts
NOUN.why: The last part (head) gives the gender and the plural, the parts before it narrow the meaning; linker = the joining element (Blume-n-kohl, Geburt-s-tag) or “−e” when the first part loses its final e (Kirsch-tomate). A verb as modifier appears as its stem (wohnen → Wohnzimmer). none: a simple or derived word, or two separate words.

NOUN.title: same form, other gender
NOUN.why: der Junge (boy) / das Junge (young animal): the article alone tells two words apart. senses: when the other gender belongs to a meaning of this word.

NOUN.title: forms of one meaning
NOUN.why: A meaning used in a form or construction of its own besides its plural (Frau as a title: Frau Weber, never plural; Bad in place names: in Bad Ems). none: every meaning uses the same forms.

VERB.title: principal parts
VERB.why: infinitive – 3rd person singular present – 3rd person singular Präteritum – Partizip II: the four forms every learner memorizes (separable verbs with the particle in place: kommt an, kam an, angekommen).

VERB.title: conjugation class
VERB.why: weak: -te, ge-…-t (kaufen); strong: vowel change, ge-…-en (trinken – trank – getrunken); mixed: vowel change with weak endings (rennen – rannte – gerannt); modal: modal verbs (mögen, wollen); irregular: sein, haben.

VERB.title: vowel change in the present (du / er)
VERB.why: essen → du isst, fahren → du fährst, laufen → du läufst; decides the du-forms and the du-imperative (iss!).

VERB.title: perfect auxiliary
VERB.why: sein for movement and change of state (ist gegangen), haben for the rest; both: it depends on the meaning or on a direct object (hat das Auto gefahren / ist nach Berlin gefahren) – see auxBySense.

VERB.title: auxiliary per meaning
VERB.why: For verbs with aux “both”: which meaning (or construction) takes which auxiliary. none: one auxiliary for every meaning.

VERB.title: separable particle
VERB.why: The stressed particle goes to the end of the clause (Ich komme morgen an), ge- and zu go inside it (angekommen, anzukommen).

VERB.title: inseparable prefix
VERB.why: An unstressed prefix that never separates and takes no ge- in the participle (verlassen – verlassen).

VERB.title: objects and complements, per meaning
VERB.why: The case of each object (helfen + DAT, kaufen + ACC (+ DAT)), a preposition the verb chooses (warten auf + ACC), or a predicative nominative (Ich heiße Anna). none: the verb takes no object in any meaning.

VERB.title: reflexive use, per meaning
VERB.why: A meaning that needs the reflexive pronoun (sich verlassen auf: ich verlasse mich). none: no reflexive meaning.

VERB.title: manner of motion
VERB.why: German chooses the verb by how one moves: gehen (on foot), fahren (in a vehicle), fliegen (by air); kommen, reisen say nothing about it.

VERB.title: forms of one meaning
VERB.why: A meaning that uses forms of its own (mögen “would like” → möchte, möchtest …). none: every meaning uses the same forms.

ADJ.title: comparison
ADJ.why: regular: klein – kleiner – am kleinsten; umlaut: alt – älter – am ältesten; irregular: gut – besser – am besten, hoch – höher; not compared: rosa, lila. The forms are in ADJ;CMPR and ADJ;SPRL.

ADJ.title: stem before an ending
ADJ.why: Some adjectives change before an ending: hoch → hoh- (ein hoher Turm), dunkel → dunkl-, teuer → teur-. none: the ending is added to the base form (or the word takes no endings).

ADV.title: comparative and superlative
ADV.why: Some adverbs compare: oft – öfter – am öftesten, bald – eher – am ehesten. none: not compared (or itself a comparative / superlative form).

ADP.title: case, per meaning
ADP.why: Every preposition decides the case of its noun; the two-way prepositions (in, an, auf …) take the dative for where? and the accusative for where to?, and some meanings take only one (über “about” + ACC, am Montag + DAT). A meaning that is not prepositional (zu “too”, auf “open”) is in no item. A contraction (im, zum) states the case of its article; senses: omitted.

ADP.title: merged with the article
ADP.why: in + dem = im, zu + der = zur; some merged forms are colloquial (unterm, übers). none: no merged forms, or the word is itself a merged form.

DET.title: adjective endings after it
DET.why: der-words → weak endings (der gute Wein), ein-words → mixed (ein guter Wein), words that show no case themselves → strong (viel guter Wein, einige gute Freunde).

DET.title: addressee
DET.why: dein / euer (du, ihr) or Ihr (Sie). none: the owner is not the person spoken to.

DET.title: forms of one meaning
DET.why: A meaning with forms of its own (ein standing alone → einer, eine, eins). none: every meaning uses the same forms.

PRON.title: addressee
PRON.why: du / ihr (informal) or Sie (formal). none: not a pronoun of address.

PRON.title: what it refers to
PRON.why: er / sie / es refer to things as well, by the gender of the noun (der Tisch → er); wer asks for persons, was for things.

PRON.title: forms of one meaning
PRON.why: A meaning with forms of its own (das Ich, die Ichs; Ihr written with a capital). none: every meaning uses the same forms.

NUM.title: ordinal (der …)
NUM.why: The ordinal adjective: -te up to 19 (der zweite), -ste from 20 (der zwanzigste); irregular erste, dritte, siebte (also siebente), achte.

SCONJ.title: position of the finite verb
values: at the end of its clause
SCONJ.why: A subordinating conjunction sends the finite verb to the end of its clause (…, weil ich Hunger habe).

CCONJ.title: effect on word order
CCONJ.why: und, oder, aber, denn stand before the clause and change nothing (…, denn ich habe Hunger); weder / noch take the first place, so the verb follows them (Weder hat er angerufen, noch …).

INTJ.title: formality
INTJ.why: Which situations the formula fits: informal (friends, family: hallo, tschüss), formal (strangers, customers: guten Tag, auf Wiedersehen, wie geht es Ihnen), neutral (both).
